passage: Arnab had worked at the same bank branch in Salt Lake for three years. His manager was kind, the pay was fine, and he could process a loan file with his eyes shut. That was the problem. He had started scrolling through his phone between customers, forgetting what he'd scrolled. At home he snapped at nothing. "You're not sick, you're bored," said Kalyani from the next counter, when he sighed for the fourth time before lunch. Then she mentioned that the branch was starting a money-basics workshop for small shopkeepers and needed someone to design the sessions. Arnab volunteered that afternoon. For the next month he stayed late making charts and practising in front of the mirror. He was tired. He felt more awake than he had in a year.

'Remember your evening course in graphic design? You'd come home at ten and still talk for an hour.'

Usha was quiet. Then she smiled a little. 'I could offer to redesign it. I'd have to learn half of it.'
'That's the point.'

I had a steady job checking shipping invoices at a logistics office in Pune, good colleagues, a canteen that makes decent vada pav. But every day was the same forty invoices. I stopped reading books. I slept a lot on weekends and still felt tired. When my friend Nikita asked how work was, I said, "Easy," and she said, "That's not what easy looks like." She sent me a link to a weekend course in data analysis. I nearly didn't sign up. Now, three months in, my brain actually hurts on Saturdays, in a good way. I even built a small dashboard at work, and my manager asked how I did it. I feel charged again.

Anushree (25) has been with us three years. Her work is accurate and on time. Nothing is wrong. But this month I noticed she sighs at the returns trolley, eats lunch alone at her desk scrolling, and on Tuesday she said to me, 'I could do this job asleep. Some days I think I am.'

Sunday night
Another week of the same forty test cases. Pass, pass, pass. Good pay, nice team, a manager who says thank you. And I feel like old rice. Nothing's wrong, which is the annoying part. What am I even complaining about?
Chetan came over for chai and I said it out loud for the first time. He didn't tell me to be grateful. He said, 'Saurabh, when did you last learn something at work?' I actually couldn't remember. Maybe eighteen months ago.
He's doing an evening course in embedded systems and made me look at the syllabus. Something woke up in my chest reading it. Microcontrollers! I used to love that stuff in college.
Signed up. Starts Tuesday. First time in months I'm looking forward to a weekday.

Subject: Something I can't quite explain

Jaya,

You asked why I sounded low on the phone. Nothing is wrong, really. That's the strange part.

I've been at the bank branch for three years. I'm good at it. I process loan files faster than anyone. My manager is kind. The pay is fine.

But I wake up flat. Every day is the same set of forms, and I could do them asleep. I catch myself scrolling job sites at lunch without applying anywhere. I'm restless in a way I can't point at.

Last week they asked for a volunteer to help design the new customer-training workshop. I put my hand up without thinking. For the first time in months, I stayed late and didn't notice the time.

Maybe I'm not tired of work. Maybe I'm tired of not learning anything.

Himani

I'm Nazia. I've been doing payroll at the same firm since I was twenty-two. Same spreadsheet, same dates, same questions every month. I'm fast. I'm accurate. I'm fine.

Rehana, from the network team, came in with a torch. "Deepak, we need someone to help test the new fibre routers this month. It's messy. Nobody knows the system yet. Interested?" He almost said no out of habit. Then he felt something he hadn't felt in months: a small spark of curiosity. "Yes." For the next three weeks he stayed late in the router room, reading manuals and making mistakes. He was tired. But he was humming again. On Friday he told Rehana, "I think I was bored, not tired."
